name: White Hole, the Lagging Core of Novikov and Ne'eman
description: A ball of dust that comes out of a singularity through the past horizon of Schwarzschild's exterior, Oppenheimer and Snyder's collapse with the time reversed. Igor Novikov and Yuval Ne'eman proposed it in 1964 and 1965 as a piece of the big bang that started late, and as what a quasar is.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ is the Schwarzschild radius of the core. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: The energy of the quasars was a puzzle in 1964, and the attempts on it began with gravitational collapse [novikov1965]. Igor Novikov tried the opposite [novikov1964, novikov1965]. Could a quasar be a piece of the big bang that started late? He took a Friedmann universe of dust and held some of its cores back, each one waiting inside its own Schwarzschild sphere while the universe expanded around it, and each coming out at a time of its own [novikov1965]. He called the motion "anticollapse" [novikov1965].¶His solution is exact: each core is a ball of uniform dust, the space around it is Schwarzschild's vacuum, and the whole sits in the hole that Albert Einstein and Ernst Straus cut out of a Friedmann universe in 1945 [einstein1945, novikov1965]. In coordinates that move with the dust it is Richard Tolman's solution of 1934, with the shells of the core leaving the singularity later than the universe around them [tolman1934, novikov1965]. A core with too little energy to escape rises to a largest size and falls back, and that one is J. Robert Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder's collapsing star with the film run backwards [novikov1965, oppenheimersnyder1939].¶Novikov saw that from far away the film does not simply run backwards [novikov1965]. For a distant observer a collapsing star takes forever to reach its Schwarzschild sphere and fades as it goes [novikov1965]. The exploding core is seen from its first instant, "beginning with point dimensions" [novikov1965]. Yuval Ne'eman came to the same hypothesis independently in 1965 [neeman1965, zeldovichnovikov1967]. With Gerald Tauber he named it the lagging core model and drew it on Martin Kruskal's diagram, where the core, in their words, "seems to be emerging from an impossible past" [neemantauber1967, kruskal1960].¶The name white hole came after the idea: by 1974 Ne'eman was writing of his lagging cores as "white holes" in "presently fashionable nomenclature" [neeman1974]. Could such a core really wait? Novikov and Yakov Zel'dovich had their doubts as early as 1966: in a hot universe a body inside its Schwarzschild sphere swallows the radiation around it, and if that accretion proved catastrophic the hypothesis, they wrote, "will conflict with observational data" [zeldovichnovikov1967].¶Douglas Eardley gave the classical answer in 1974: a white hole "cannot exist, because it suffers an exponentially growing instability that converts it into a black hole" [eardley1974]. While it waits it gathers matter, and that matter turns its outgoing light back, as Kayll Lake summed up the argument, so that from outside it comes to look like a black hole [lake1978]. That same year Zel'dovich, Novikov, and Alexei Starobinsky reached the quantum answer, in which particles created near the singularity change the core so much that it "either blows up practically without delay" or "never explodes at all" [zeldovichnovikovstarobinskii1974]. They concluded that powering anything in the sky with white holes "seems extremely unlikely" [zeldovichnovikovstarobinskii1974].¶Is a white hole then just a black hole watched in a mirror? In quantum theory Stephen Hawking thought so: black holes, he wrote in 1976, "are indistinguishable, for an external observer, from white holes" [hawking1976thermo]. Robert Wald and Sriram Ramaswamy put a quantum field on a white hole four years later and found Eardley's instability again, an infinite flux of particles as the horizon ends, which they took as evidence "that the laws of quantum gravity may not be time-reversal invariant" [waldramaswamy1980]. The classical argument has held up: when Claude Barrabès, Patrick Brady, and Eric Poisson went back over it in 1993 they traced the death to the gravity of the gathered matter, as Lake, R. C. Roeder, and Steven Blau had, and kept Eardley's conclusion [barrabes1993, lakeroeder1976, blau1989]. A white hole lasts a time of order $GM/c^3$, by Amos Ori and Poisson's reckoning, and the place to catch one exploding is at high redshift [oripoisson1994].

related.text: The same ball of dust with the time reversed. After its moment of rest the white hole's core is Oppenheimer and Snyder's star, falling back [oppenheimersnyder1939].
The outside of the core. Its surface is a radial geodesic of Schwarzschild's metric that crosses $r = r_s$ outward, through the past horizon.

The inside of the core, a ball of a Friedmann universe of dust that leaves the big bang late. Novikov's own core is cut from the flat universe, and the one that falls back from the closed one [novikov1965].
Novikov's solution is Tolman's dust with no energy function, $E = 0$, and a bang that comes later for the core than for the shells around it [tolman1934, novikov1965].
The vacuum inside the past horizon, between the singularity and the dust, is Kantowski and Sachs's vacuum universe with its spheres growing, the region Novikov called a T region [novikov1965].
A white hole that sends out light. Zel'dovich, Novikov, and Starobinsky used Vaidya's metric for the radiation leaving one [zeldovichnovikovstarobinskii1974, vaidya1953].

coordinates.name: Comoving Dust Interior

parameters.description: Scale factor of the dust, a length ($a > 0$), obeying $2a\ddot{a}+\dot{a}^2+1 = 0$, which the cycloid $a = a_m\sin^2(\eta/2)$, $c\tau = \frac{a_m}{2}(\eta - \sin\eta)$ solves

Comoving polar angle of the core's surface ($0 < \chi_0 < \pi/2$), fixed by its compactness at the moment of rest through $\sin^2\chi_0 = r_s/R_0$, where $R_0 = a_m\sin\chi_0$ is the largest areal radius the surface reaches
Scale factor at the moment of rest, the maximum of the cycloid, tied to the exterior mass by $r_s = a_m\sin^3\chi_0$

coordinates.convention: We use comoving coordinates $(\tau, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, where $\tau$ is the proper time of the dust since it left its singularity, $\chi$ is a dimensionless comoving polar angle, and the scale factor $a(\tau)$ carries the length, and the core is the ball $\chi \le \chi_0$. The scale factor leaves $a = 0$ at $\tau = 0$, comes to rest at $a_m$ at $\tau = \dfrac{\pi a_m}{2c}$, and returns to $a = 0$ at $\tau = \dfrac{\pi a_m}{c}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, a dot on the scale factor is $\dot{a} = \dfrac{da}{d(c\tau)} = \dfrac{1}{c}\dfrac{da}{d\tau}$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Conformal Time Interior

parameters.description: Comoving polar angle of the core's surface ($0 < \chi_0 < \pi/2$), fixed by its compactness at the moment of rest through $\sin^2\chi_0 = r_s/R_0$, where $R_0 = a_m\sin\chi_0$ is the largest areal radius the surface reaches
Scale factor at the moment of rest, the maximum of the cycloid, tied to the exterior mass by $r_s = a_m\sin^3\chi_0$

coordinates.convention: We use the conformal time $\eta$ of the dust, a dimensionless parameter along the cycloid with $a = a_m\sin^2(\eta/2)$ and $c\tau = \frac{a_m}{2}(\eta - \sin\eta)$ for its proper time $\tau$, and the comoving polar angle $\chi$, and the core is the ball $\chi \le \chi_0$. The dust leaves its singularity at $\eta = 0$, is at rest at $\eta = \pi$, and falls back to $\eta = 2\pi$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Schwarzschild Exterior

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the core, $r_s = 2GM/c^2 = a_m\sin^3\chi_0$

coordinates.convention: We use Schwarzschild coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $t = 0$ at the moment of rest, and $R(t)$ is the areal radius of the surface of the core. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein Exterior

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the core, $r_s = 2GM/c^2 = a_m\sin^3\chi_0$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, where the retarded time $u$ is a length, constant along each outgoing ray and counted from the ray the surface sends as it crosses $r_s$ on its way out, so $u$ differs from $ct - r - r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$ by a constant. The areal radius of the surface of the core is $R(u)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Kruskal Exterior

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the core, $r_s = 2GM/c^2 = a_m\sin^3\chi_0$

Areal radius, a length, the solution of $\left(1 - r/r_s\right)e^{r/r_s} = UV$, with $\mathrm{W}$ the principal branch of Lambert's function, $\mathrm{W}(x)\,e^{\mathrm{W}(x)} = x$; its derivatives are $\partial_U r = -r_s^2\,V e^{-r/r_s}/r$ and $\partial_V r = -r_s^2\,U e^{-r/r_s}/r$

coordinates.convention: We use Kruskal's null coordinates $(U, V, \theta, \phi)$, with $U$ and $V$ numbers, and outside $r_s$ they are $U = -e^{-u/2r_s}$ and $V = e^{v/2r_s}$ for the retarded time $u$ counted from the surface's crossing of $r_s$ on its way out and the advanced time $v = u + 2r + 2r_s\ln(r/r_s - 1)$. The areal radius $r$ is a function of $UV$, with $\mathrm{W}$ Lambert's function, and $R$ is the areal radius of the surface of the core. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Novikov's Comoving
domains: ct > b \;\text{(after the shell leaves its singularity)}

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass inside the shell $r$, a length: $F = 2GM(r)/c^2$, an arbitrary function of $r$ alone that never decreases, constant across a vacuum. The prime is $F' = dF/dr$.

Delay of the shell $r$, a length: the shell leaves its singularity at $ct = b(r)$, later where $b$ is larger. A uniform Friedmann universe has $b$ constant, and the shells do not cross where $q\,F' - 2F\,b' > 0$. The prime is $b' = db/dr$.
Proper time of the shell $r$ since it left its singularity, times $c$, a length
Areal radius, a length: the shell $r$ has area $4\pi R^2$ at time $t$. Its derivatives are $\partial_t R = 2R/3q$ along $x^0 = ct$ and $\partial_r R = R\left(q\,F' - 2F\,b'\right)/3Fq$.

coordinates.convention: We use Novikov's comoving coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ the proper time of the dust and of the freely moving shells of the vacuum, and $r$ a label, a length, that each shell keeps. The shell $r$ leaves its singularity at $ct = b(r)$ and has the areal radius $R$, and the Schwarzschild radius of the mass inside it is $F(r)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
